text: Julie Mehretu (born November 28, 1970) is an Ethiopian American contemporary visual artist renowned for her large-scale, multi-layered abstract paintings that depict the cumulative effects of urban sociopolitical changes. Born in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, she is the first child of a geography professor and a Jewish American Montessori teacher, and fled the country in 1977 due to political turmoil, relocating to East Lansing, Michigan, for her father’s teaching position at Michigan State University. She graduated from East Lansing High School, earned a Bachelor of Arts from Kalamazoo College, completed a junior year abroad at Cheikh Anta Diop University in Dakar, Senegal, and received a Master of Fine Arts from the Rhode Island School of Design in 1997. She was a resident of the CORE Program at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston (1997–98) and the Artist-in-Residence Program at the Studio Museum in Harlem (2001), and also participated in a residency at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis in 2003, where she worked with thirty high school girls from East Africa. In 2007, she was the Guna S. Mundheim Visual Arts Fellow at the American Academy in Berlin and later led a monthlong residency with 40 Detroit public high school art students. During her time in Berlin, she was commissioned by the Deutsche Guggenheim to create seven paintings titled Grey Area (2008–2009), which explore Berlin’s history of destruction and regeneration, featuring techniques such as erasure and translucent overlays of nineteenth-century building facades. Her work includes pieces like Vanescere (2007), Fragment (2008–09), Middle Grey (2007–09), and Berliner Plätze (2008–09). Mehretu’s paintings incorporate technical drawings of urban buildings, city grids, and weather charts, using multiple perspectives and layered forms to create flattened, abstracted representations of city life. Her drawings, often smaller in scale, serve as exploratory works between larger paintings. In 2002, she described her mark-making as a sign language for characters with social agency, charting their cities, conflicts, and development in an abstracted, intangible space. Notable works include Imperial Construction, Istanbul (2004), Stadia I, II, and III (2004), Mogamma: A Painting in Four Parts (2012), The Round City, Hatshepsut (2013), and Insile (2013). In 2007, Goldman Sachs commissioned a $5 million lobby mural, Mural, which measured the size of a tennis court and combined financial maps, architectural drawings, and references to other artists, praised by Calvin Tomkins of the New Yorker and other commentators as one of the largest and most successful public artworks. Mehretu has experimented with printmaking since graduate school, working with studios such as Highpoint Editions, Crown Point Press, Gemini G.E.L., and Derrière L'Étoile Studios and Burnet Editions. She received the Foundation for Contemporary Arts Grants to Artists Award in 2000, the Penny McCall Award in 2001, and the MacArthur Fellowship in 2005. In 2013, she received the Barnett and Annalee Newman Award and in 2015, the US Department of State Medal of Arts from Secretary John Kerry. In 2020, Time magazine included her in its list of the 100 most influential people, and in 2023, she was among the top ten in contemporary auction prices for women artists. In 2016, she created the diptych HOWL, eon (I, II) (2016–2017) for the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, which was first exhibited publicly on September 2, 2017, and developed in a decommissioned church in Harlem with collaboration from jazz pianist Jason Moran. The work is a political commentary on the Western United States’ landscape, including the San Francisco Bay Area, using digitally abstracted images of race riots, protests, and the American West. In 2021, the Whitney Museum of American Art held a full-floor retrospective of her career. Her work is included in the 2024 exhibition Every Sound Is a Shape of Time at the Pérez Art Museum Miami. In 2024, her first painted glass artwork, Uprising of the Sun (85 feet tall), was installed as a window in the Barack Obama Presidential Center, inspired by a quote from Obama about the Selma marches. In 2024, she also created the 20th BMW art car (BMW M Hybrid V8), which bore the number 20 for the 24 Hours of Le Mans, crashed early, was repaired overnight, and finished. Her painting Untitled 1 (2001) sold for $1.02 million at Sotheby's in 2010 (estimated $600–$800,000), Mumbo Jumbo (2008) sold for $5 million at White Cube in 2014, and Walkers With the Dawn and Morning (2008) sold for $10.7 million in 2023, setting a record for an African-born artist. In 2005, her work was central to the Lehmann v. The Project Worldwide case, the first legal case involving a collector’s right to first refusal in contemporary art, which revealed pricing and discount practices in the art market. In October 2023, her Untitled (2001) sold for $9.32 million at Sotheby's Hong Kong, breaking the auction record for an African artist. Mehretu lives in a two-story house in Harlem, married artist Jessica Rankin in 2008 (with whom she has two children, Cade Elias born in 2005 and Haile born in 2011; her mother-in-law is Lily Brett), and separated in 2014. She maintains a studio in Chelsea near the Whitney Museum and co-founded Denniston Hill in 2004 with Lawrence Chua and Paul Pfeiffer. She worked from an old arms factory in Berlin in 2007 and from the former St. Thomas the Apostle Church in Harlem from 2016 to 2017. In October 2024, she donated over two million dollars to the Whitney Museum’s "Free 25 and Under" program. Mehretu is a member of the Artists Committee of Americans for the Arts and has participated in numerous group exhibitions, including Painting at the Edge of the World (2001), the 2004–05 Carnegie International, the Freestyle exhibition at the Studio Museum in Harlem (2001), The Americans at the Barbican Gallery (2001), White Cube (2002), the Busan Biennale (2002), the 8th Baltic Triennial (2002), Drawing Now: Eight Propositions (2002), In Praise of Doubt (2011), dOCUMENTA (13) (2012), and The Divine Comedy: Heaven, Purgatory and Hell Revisited (2014). The first exhibition dedicated to her in Australia and the Asia-Pacific region, A Transcore of the Radical Imaginatory, was held at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia, Sydney, from November 2024 to April 2025.
